blocks.text: 2.4.1 Defining and Using Records in Java

The report service caches rendered PDFs in a `HashMap`, keyed by `record CacheKey(String tenant, byte[] digest)`, where `digest` is the SHA-256 of the report's parameters. The cache has never had a hit. Each request computes the digest, builds a key, misses, renders the PDF again and adds one more entry, and the debug log prints keys like `CacheKey[tenant=acme, digest=[B@4d405ef7]`.

A record is a class whose state is the list of components in its header. From that list the compiler writes a private final field and an accessor for each component (unit 2.2.2), a canonical constructor that takes them in order, and `equals`, `hashCode` and `toString`. Every output is from Java 21.
A Record's equals Compares Each Component with Its Own equals, So an Array Compares by Identity
record CacheKey(String tenant, byte[] digest) {}

lookup: null
equals: false
key: CacheKey[tenant=acme, digest=[B@4d405ef7]

The generated `equals` holds when the argument is the same record class and every pair of components is equal. A reference component is compared with `Objects.equals`, a primitive with its wrapper's `compare` (the `Record.equals` javadoc). `hashCode` combines the components' hash codes, and `toString` prints each component's own `toString`. An array inherits `equals` and `hashCode` from `Object`, so two digests holding the same 32 bytes are two different keys. A `List<Byte>` component would compare by contents, because `List.equals` does.

Every request renders, and every request adds an entry that no lookup finds, until the heap runs out. Either store a type that compares by value, such as the digest as a hex `String`, or override `equals` and `hashCode` with `Arrays.equals` and `Arrays.hashCode` (and `toString` with `Arrays.toString`). An array is also mutable, so copy it on the way in, as unit 1.3.3 does for a list, and return a copy from the accessor, which otherwise hands out the field. Once `hashCode` reads the contents, a caller that changes the array after `put` changes the key's hash, and the entry is lost in the map.
<!-- practice 1 -->
The Compact Constructor Runs Before the Fields Are Assigned, So It Checks the Parameters
A compact constructor is the canonical constructor without its parameter list. Its body sees the components as parameters, and when the body ends, the compiler assigns each parameter to its field.
Spot the Problem: a Check That Never Fires
`System.out.println("accessors: " + new Interval(9, 4))` prints:

in the body: Interval[start=0, end=0]
accessors: Interval[start=9, end=4]

While the body runs, the fields hold their defaults, so the accessors return 0 and the inverted interval goes through. Any instance method called from the body sees the same zeros and nulls, so a check that calls a method on a reference component's accessor throws `NullPointerException`. Written against the parameters, `if (end < start)`, the same constructor throws `IllegalArgumentException: 9 > 4`.

`javac` refuses the other ways to reach the fields: `this.start = ...` in the body is `cannot assign a value to final variable start`, and reading `this.start` is `variable start might not have been initialized`. To change a value before it is stored, assign the parameter, as unit 2.2.2 does with `name = name.strip().toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT)`. Check the value after normalising it: a check for an empty name placed before `strip()` lets `"   "` through, and stores it as `""`.
A Custom Constructor Must Call the Canonical One First, So Checks Belong in the Canonical One
This `Interval` parses `"4-9"`, and checks the order in the constructor that parses:

text:      java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: 9-4
canonical: Interval[start=9, end=4]

`new Interval("9-4")` is refused, and `new Interval(9, 4)` is not. A record may have other constructors, but each must start with `this(...)`. One that assigns the fields itself fails with `constructor is not canonical, so its first statement must invoke another constructor of class Interval`. Every path to a record therefore ends in the canonical constructor: `new` with all components, the other constructors, and Java serialization, which calls the canonical constructor and nothing else (unit 2.2.3 shows it refusing a forged stream).

A check placed after `this(...)`, or in a factory, guards only the callers of that one path. Code that builds an `Interval` from two database columns, or deserializes one from a queue, gets past it. Put every check in the canonical constructor, compact or explicit, and let the other constructors only convert their arguments.
<!-- practice 2 -->
A Record's Body Adds Methods, Static Members and Interfaces, but No Instance Field

[c-17, s-03, s-01]
[Vendor[id=s-02, country=BE], Vendor[id=s-09, country=NL]]

`Customer` has no body and still implements `Identified`: its generated accessor `id()` is public with the interface method's signature, so it is the implementation. `java.lang.Record`, which every record extends, declares only `equals`, `hashCode` and `toString`. An instance field can't go in the body: `private int hits;` is `field declaration must be static`, and `javac` suggests a record component instead. All instance state is in the header, so all of it passes through the canonical constructor and takes part in `equals`, `hashCode` and `toString`. A record can't extend a class; unit 2.4.3 covers what that rules out.
Nested and Local Records Are Static, So They Can't Reach an Outer Instance or a Local Variable

A record nested in a class is implicitly `static`: a `Line` has no enclosing `Order`, so `new Order.Line("TEA-1", 450)` works from a static method, and there is no `currency` to read. A record declared in a method is static too, unlike a local class or a lambda, so it can't capture the method's variables, even effectively final ones:

A hidden reference to an outer object or a captured variable would be state outside the header, missing from the constructor and from `equals`. Make it a component: with `record Slot(int start, int width)` and `new Slot(s, width)`, `labels(List.of(0, 30), 15)` returns `[0-15, 30-45]`.
<!-- practice 3 -->
Summary

items: **`equals`, `hashCode` and `toString` use each component's own methods.** An array component compares by identity; store a value type or override all three with `Arrays`.
**The compact constructor runs before the fields are assigned.** Check and normalise the parameters; accessors and `this` see default values there.
**Every constructor ends in the canonical one, and so does Java deserialization.** A check anywhere else guards one path.
**The body adds methods, static members and interfaces, never instance fields.** A matching accessor implements an interface method.
**Nested and local records are static.** Pass what they need as components.

blocks.text: Reference
**What a record declaration generates (Java 21):**

rows: `private final`, assigned once, by the canonical constructor
`public`, returns the field; an explicit one must be `public` with the component's type
parameters in header order; explicit or compact, at least as accessible as the record
same record class, and each component equal as below
combines the components' hashes; the formula is unspecified
`Name[c1=v1, c2=v2]`; the javadoc says the format may change, so don't parse it

blocks.text: **How the generated `equals` compares one component (ran):**

rows: by contents if the type's `equals` is; `null` equals `null`
equal contents, different arrays: not equal

blocks.text: **What `javac` 21 refuses:**

rows: `cannot assign a value to final variable c`
`variable c might not have been initialized`
another constructor that doesn't start with `this(...)`
`constructor is not canonical, so its first statement must invoke another constructor of class R`
an instance field in the body
a canonical constructor less accessible than the record
`invalid canonical constructor in record R` (`attempting to assign stronger access privileges`)
a nested or local record reading an outer field or local variable
`non-static variable x cannot be referenced from a static context`

blocks.text: Challenges

items: For the cache key above, would you store the digest as a hex `String`, a `ByteBuffer`, or keep `byte[]` and override three methods? Measure each on a million lookups.
A record has twelve components and four of them are optional. Do you add constructors, static factories or a builder, and where does each one's validation run?

A library reads and writes your records by reflection, through their accessors and canonical constructor. Which of this page's rules does it rely on, and what breaks if a record overrides an accessor?

blocks.text: Design Note: Why a Record Compares Arrays by Identity

The generated methods are defined by the components alone: `equals` asks each component's `equals`, with no exception for arrays. An exception would make an array equal by contents inside a record while the same array in a `List` or a map value is not, and the generated `hashCode` would hash every byte of a large array on each call. The cost is that a record holding an array has value syntax and identity equality, and `javac` gives no warning.
